title: GIS-BASED MORPHOMETRIC CHARACTERIZATION AND WATERSHED MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS: A CASE STUDY OF MABACAN WATERSHED, PHILIPPINES

GIS-BASED MORPHOMETRIC CHARACTERIZATION AND WATERSHED MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS: A CASE STUDY OF MABACAN WATERSHED, PHILIPPINES

Journal: Water Conservation and Management (WCM)
Author: Arlene B. Tolentino, Edwin R. Abucay, Rico C. Ancog, Joan Pauline P. Talubo, Victor B. Ella
Print ISSN : 2523-5664

ABSTRACT

Morphometric characterization offers a practical means of determining the watershed form and drainage organization especially in areas where hydrological and field observations are limited. This study utilized geographic information system (GIS) techniques and a 30-m Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) digital elevation model (DEM) to characterize the Mabacan watershed in Laguna and Batangas, Philippines. The watershed was delineated using ArcHydro tools in ArcGIS 10.5, with the Mabacan River channel digitized from Google Earth and incorporated into the DEM-based workflow to improve channel alignment. Morphometric characteristics were examined looking at the linear, areal, and relief parameters for the 13 subbasins. The watershed has a third-order drainage basin dominated by first-order streams. Its drainage network shows a predominantly parallel pattern, while the mean bifurcation ratio of 1.86 indicates relatively limited structural irregularity in the extracted network. The watershed has a drainage density of 0.72 km/km2, a stream frequency of 0.53 km2, an elongation ratio of 0.48, and a circularity ratio of 0.09, showing an elongate basin form. At the subbasin scale, the geological behavior is spatially heterogeneous. On the other hand, subbasins 4, 5, and 10 have relatively high drainage density and stream frequency. Subbasin 2, 6, and 9 have comparatively high relief ratios that warrant greater attention to erosion and slope-related process. Overall, results show that morphometric information is most useful when assessed alongside terrain and land cover characteristics, rather than as a stand-alone predictor of hydrological response. The study illustrates how GIS-based morphometric assessment can provide a cost-effective basis for differentiating conservation, runoff management, groundwater recharge, and land use planning priorities within data-scarce watersheds.
